claim: S. cerevisiae cells regulate carbon and nitrogen metabolic homeostasis through tRNA U34-thiolation.
source: Here, we report that S. cerevisiae cells regulate carbon and nitrogen metabolic homeostasis through tRNA U34-thiolation.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract, supported by multiple experimental results throughout the manuscript including metabolic flux experiments, metabolite measurements, and genetic analyses.

claim: Despite amino acid sufficiency, tRNA-thiolation deficient cells appear amino acid starved.
source: Despite amino acid sufficiency, tRNA-thiolation deficient cells appear amino acid starved.
evidence: Supported by data showing increased intracellular amino acid pools (Figure 1A) and increased Gcn4 protein levels (Figure 1C) in thiolation mutants.

claim: In tRNA thiolation deficient cells, carbon flux towards nucleotide synthesis decreases.
source: In these cells, carbon flux towards nucleotide synthesis decreases, and trehalose synthesis increases, resulting in a starvation-like metabolic signature.
evidence: Demonstrated by 13C-glucose labeling experiments showing decreased label incorporation into nucleotides (Figure 2B, 2C) and 15N-ammonium sulfate labeling showing decreased nitrogen incorporation into nucleotides (Figure 1E).

claim: In tRNA thiolation deficient cells, trehalose synthesis increases.
source: In these cells, carbon flux towards nucleotide synthesis decreases, and trehalose synthesis increases, resulting in a starvation-like metabolic signature.
evidence: Supported by increased steady-state trehalose levels (Figure 2E) and increased 13C-glucose label incorporation into trehalose (Figure 2F) in thiolation mutants.

claim: Thiolation mutants have only minor translation defects.
source: Thiolation mutants have only minor translation defects.
evidence: Supported by ribosome profiling data showing exceptional correlation (R2 >0.97) between WT and thiolation mutants for both transcripts and ribosome footprints (Figure 4A, 4B), with only modest increases in ribosome densities at codons recognized by thiolated tRNAs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).

claim: In tRNA thiolation mutants, phosphate homeostasis genes are strongly down-regulated.
source: However, in these cells phosphate homeostasis genes are strongly down-regulated, resulting in an effectively phosphate-limited state.
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq and ribosome profiling showing ~20 PHO regulon genes strongly downregulated (p<10−7) in thiolation mutants (Figure 4E, 4F), and confirmed by Western blot analysis of Pho12 and Pho84 proteins (Figure 5B, 5C).

claim: Reduced phosphate in thiolation mutants enforces a metabolic switch where glucose-6-phosphate is routed towards storage carbohydrates.
source: Reduced phosphate enforces a metabolic switch, where glucose-6-phosphate is routed towards storage carbohydrates.
evidence: Supported by increased trehalose and glycogen levels (Figure 2E), increased trehalose synthesis flux (Figure 2F), and decreased nucleotide synthesis (Figures 1E, 2B, 2C) in thiolation mutants with dampened PHO response.

claim: Trehalose synthesis releases phosphate and thereby restores phosphate availability.
source: Notably, trehalose synthesis, which releases phosphate and thereby restores phosphate availability, is central to this metabolic rewiring.
evidence: Demonstrated by the Tps2-mediated dephosphorylation reaction releasing free Pi (Figure 7A), intracellular Pi measurements showing dramatic reduction in uba4Δ tps2Δ double mutants (Figure 7B), and synthetic genetic interactions between TPS2 and thiolation genes (Figure 7C).

claim: Cells use thiolated tRNAs to perceive amino acid sufficiency and balance carbon and amino acid metabolic flux by controlling phosphate availability.
source: Thus, cells use thiolated tRNAs to perceive amino acid sufficiency, balance carbon and amino acid metabolic flux and grow optimally, by controlling phosphate availability.
evidence: This is an integrative conclusion supported by multiple lines of evidence: coupling of tRNA thiolation with methionine availability (Laxman et al., 2013), metabolic rewiring in thiolation mutants, downregulation of PHO genes, and rescue experiments with TPS2.

claim: Intracellular pools of amino acids are increased in tRNA thiolation mutants.
source: Intracellular pools of amino acids are increased in tRNA thiolation mutants.
evidence: Directly measured by targeted LC-MS/MS showing significant increases in most amino acids in uba4Δ and ncs2Δ mutants compared to WT (Figure 1A).

claim: Gcn4 protein is increased in tRNA thiolation mutants.
source: Gcn4 protein is increased in tRNA thiolation mutants.
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis showing increased Gcn4-HA protein levels in uba4Δ, ncs2Δ, and ncs6Δ cells compared to WT (Figure 1C).

claim: GCN4 translation is increased in tRNA thiolation mutants.
source: GCN4 translation is increased in tRNA thiolation mutants.
evidence: Shown by luciferase reporter assays with Gcn4-luciferase constructs demonstrating higher luciferase activity in uba4Δ and ncs2Δ cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).

claim: GCN4 translation is Gcn2-dependent in tRNA thiolation mutants.
source: GCN4 translation is Gcn2-dependent in tRNA thiolation mutants.
evidence: Demonstrated by luciferase assays showing that gcn2Δ uba4Δ and gcn2Δ ncs2Δ double mutants have similar Gcn4 translation levels to gcn2Δ alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Phosphorylated eIF2α protein levels are increased in tRNA thiolation mutants.
source: Phosphorylated eIF2α (P-eIF2α) protein levels are increased in tRNA thiolation mutants.
evidence: Shown by Western blot analysis detecting increased P-eIF2α in uba4Δ, ncs2Δ, and ncs6Δ cells compared to WT (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Intracellular levels of nucleotides are decreased in tRNA thiolation mutants.
source: Intracellular levels of nucleotides are decreased in tRNA thiolation mutants.
evidence: Measured by targeted LC-MS/MS showing decreased steady-state levels of AMP, GMP, CMP, and UMP in uba4Δ cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).

claim: Total cellular ATP levels are decreased in tRNA thiolation mutants.
source: Total cellular ATP levels are decreased in tRNA thiolation mutants.
evidence: Measured using ATP determination kit showing significantly reduced ATP in uba4Δ and ncs2Δ cells compared to WT (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).

claim: Nucleotide synthesis is decreased in tRNA thiolation mutants based on nitrogen label incorporation.
source: Nucleotide synthesis is decreased in tRNA thiolation mutants (nitrogen label).
evidence: Demonstrated by 15N2-ammonium sulfate pulse-labeling experiments showing decreased label incorporation into GMP, AMP, and CMP in uba4Δ and ncs2Δ cells (Figure 1E).

claim: Amino acid synthesis is unaffected in tRNA thiolation mutants.
source: Amino acid synthesis is unaffected in tRNA thiolation mutants.
evidence: Shown by 15N2-ammonium sulfate labeling experiments demonstrating similar label incorporation into aspartate and glutamine in WT and thiolation mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).

claim: tRNA thiolation mutants exhibit increased sensitivity to 8-azaadenine.
source: tRNA thiolation mutants exhibit increased sensitivity to 8-azaadenine.
evidence: Demonstrated by spotting assay showing reduced growth of uba4Δ and ncs2Δ cells on plates containing 300 μg/ml 8-azaadenine (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).

claim: Expression of nucleotide biosynthetic genes is increased in thiolation mutants.
source: Expression of nucleotide biosynthetic genes is increased in thiolation mutants.
evidence: Shown by qRT-PCR analysis demonstrating upregulation of IMD2, URA2, URA8, ADE12, BAS1, and HPT1 in ncs2Δ cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).

claim: Nucleotide synthesis is decreased in tRNA thiolation mutants based on carbon label incorporation.
source: Nucleotide synthesis is decreased in tRNA thiolation mutant (carbon label).
evidence: Demonstrated by [U-13C6]-glucose pulse-labeling showing decreased label incorporation into GMP and AMP in ncs2Δ cells (Figure 2B).

claim: ADP and ATP synthesis is decreased in the thiolation mutant.
source: ADP and ATP synthesis is decreased in the thiolation mutant.
evidence: Shown by [U-13C6]-glucose pulse-labeling experiments demonstrating reduced 13C-label incorporation into ADP and ATP in uba4Δ cells (Figure 2C).

claim: PPP flux is decreased in the tRNA thiolation mutant.
source: PPP flux is decreased in the tRNA thiolation mutant.
evidence: Demonstrated by [U-13C6]-glucose pulse-labeling (2 min) showing decreased 13C6-label incorporation into ribose-5-phosphate in uba4Δ cells (Figure 2D).

claim: Steady-state trehalose and glycogen amounts are increased in tRNA thiolation mutants.
source: Steady-state trehalose and glycogen amounts are increased in tRNA thiolation mutants.
evidence: Measured by colorimetric assays showing significantly increased trehalose and glycogen content in uba4Δ and ncs2Δ cells compared to WT (Figure 2E).

claim: Trehalose synthesis is increased in tRNA thiolation mutant.
source: Trehalose synthesis is increased in tRNA thiolation mutant.
evidence: Demonstrated by [U-13C6]-glucose pulse-labeling showing increased label incorporation into M+6 and M+12 trehalose isotopomers in ncs2Δ cells (Figure 2F).

claim: Thiolation mutants exhibit reduced methionine-induced carbon incorporation into nucleotides.
source: Thiolation mutants exhibit reduced methionine-induced carbon incorporation into nucleotides.
evidence: Shown by [U-13C6]-glucose labeling experiments in the presence of 2 mM methionine, demonstrating reduced carbon label incorporation into AMP in uba4Δ cells compared to WT (Figure 2G).

claim: Sulfur starvation in WT cells phenocopies the metabolic state of thiolation mutants.
source: Sulfur starvation phenocopies the metabolic state of thiolation mutants
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments showing that WT cells subjected to sulfur starvation exhibit increased amino acids (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), reduced nucleotides (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D), increased trehalose (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E), and strong Gcn4 induction (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F), similar to thiolation mutants.

claim: Intracellular levels of sulfur amino acid metabolites decrease in the sulfur-starved condition.
source: Intracellular levels of sulfur amino acid metabolites decrease in the sulfur-starved condition.
evidence: Measured by targeted LC-MS/MS showing significant decreases in methionine, cysteine, SAM, and SAH in WT cells shifted to sulfur-starved medium (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).

claim: In WT cells, intracellular pools of amino acids increase in the sulfur-starved condition, similar to tRNA thiolation mutants.
source: In WT cells, intracellular pools of amino acids increase in the sulfur-starved condition, similar to tRNA thiolation mutants.
evidence: Demonstrated by targeted LC-MS/MS showing increased steady-state amino acid amounts in WT cells under sulfur starvation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).

claim: In WT cells, intracellular levels of nucleotides decrease in the sulfur-starved condition similar to tRNA thiolation mutants.
source: In WT cells, intracellular levels of nucleotides decrease in the sulfur-starved similar to tRNA thiolation mutants.
evidence: Shown by targeted LC-MS/MS measurements of AMP in WT cells under sulfur starvation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).

claim: In WT cells, steady-state trehalose amounts increase in the sulfur-starved condition, similar to tRNA thiolation mutants.
source: In WT cells, steady-state trehalose amounts increase in the sulfur-starved condition, similar to tRNA thiolation mutants.
evidence: Measured by colorimetric assay showing increased trehalose content in WT cells under sulfur starvation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).

claim: In WT cells, GCN4 translation increases in sulfur amino acid limited conditions similar to tRNA thiolation mutants.
source: In WT cells, GCN4 translation increases in sulfur amino acid (methionine and cysteine) limited conditions similar to tRNA thiolation mutants.
evidence: Demonstrated by luciferase assays showing increased Gcn4-luciferase activity in WT cells shifted to sulfur amino acid limited medium (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F).

claim: tRNA thiolation mutants exhibit asynchronous cell division and disrupted yeast metabolic cycles.
source: tRNA thiolation mutants exhibit asynchronous cell division and disrupted yeast metabolic cycles.
evidence: Shown by budding index measurements in chemostat cultures demonstrating that uba4Δ cells show asynchronous cell division while WT cells show synchronized cell cycle progression (Figure 3A).

claim: tRNA thiolation mutants show delayed cell cycle progression.
source: tRNA thiolation mutants show delayed cell cycle progression.
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis showing delayed S-phase progression in uba4Δ and ncs2Δ cells after release from G1 arrest (Figure 3B).

claim: The S/G2/M phase duration is longer in tRNA thiolation mutants.
source: Cell cycle duration, distribution of G1 phase duration (red) and S/G2/M phase durations (green) for WT and tRNA thiolation mutant cells (uba4Δ and ncs2Δ) were measured in single cells using time lapse live-cell microscopy.
evidence: Measured by time-lapse live-cell microscopy showing significantly longer S/G2/M phase duration in uba4Δ and ncs2Δ cells compared to WT (Figure 3C, 3D).

claim: tRNA thiolation mutants exhibit increased HU sensitivity.
source: tRNA thiolation mutants exhibit increased HU sensitivity.
evidence: Demonstrated by spotting assay showing reduced growth of uba4Δ and ncs2Δ cells on plates containing 150 mM hydroxyurea (Figure 3E).

claim: Catalytically dead uba4 mutants exhibit increased HU sensitivity.
source: Catalytically dead uba4 mutants (C225A and C397A) exhibit increased HU sensitivity.
evidence: Shown by spotting assay demonstrating that uba4 C225A and C397A mutants have increased sensitivity to 150 mM HU (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Rad53 activation is not perturbed in tRNA thiolation mutants.
source: Rad53 activation is not perturbed in tRNA thiolation mutants.
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis showing similar Rad53 phosphorylation patterns in WT, uba4Δ, and ncs2Δ cells in the presence or absence of HU (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Very few differentially regulated genes were observed in tRNA thiolation mutants compared to WT.
source: Correlation plots are shown, for WT and tRNA thiolation mutant cells (ncs2Δ and uba4Δ), for both gene expression (transcript) and ribosome footprint (translation) changes. The coefficients of determination (R2) values are indicated, along with their significance (p values). Note: Very few differentially regulated genes were observed, and these are indicated as red points.
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq and ribosome profiling showing exceptional correlation (R2 >0.97) between WT and thiolation mutants, with fewer than ~30 genes up or downregulated at a two-fold change cutoff (Figure 4A).

claim: Overall ribosome densities for thiolation mutants correlate exceptionally well with ribosome densities in WT cells.
source: Correlation plots comparing ribosome densities (RPF TPM/RNA TPM) for the thiolation mutants (ncs2Δ or uba4Δ respectively) with WT cells. Note: overall ribosome densities for thiolation mutants correlate exceptionally well with ribosome densities in WT cells, with the correlation coefficients (R) > 0.88 in both comparisons.
evidence: Shown by correlation analysis of ribosome density data demonstrating R > 0.88 for both ncs2Δ and uba4Δ compared to WT (Figure 4B).

claim: Amino acid biosynthesis genes were upregulated in tRNA thiolation mutant cells.
source: A density plot, representing changes in expression (transcript and ribosome footprints) of genes associated with amino acid biosynthetic pathways. In general, amino acid biosynthesis genes were upregulated in tRNA thiolation mutant cells (uba4Δ and ncs2Δ).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq and ribosome profiling data showing increased transcript and ribosome footprint levels for amino acid biosynthesis genes (Figure 4C).

claim: Trehalose, glycogen biosynthesis and PPP genes were unchanged in tRNA thiolation mutant cells compared to WT cells.
source: A density plot, representing changes in expression (transcript and ribosome footprints) of genes associated with trehalose and glycogen biosynthetic pathways, and the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP). In general, trehalose, glycogen biosynthesis and PPP genes were unchanged in tRNA thiolation mutant cells (uba4Δ and ncs2Δ), compared to WT cells.
evidence: Shown by RNA-seq and ribosome profiling data demonstrating negligible changes in mRNA or ribosome-footprint abundances for these genes (Figure 4D).

claim: PHO regulon genes are strongly downregulated in tRNA thiolation mutants at both transcript and ribosome-footprint levels.
source: Heat map depicting changes in expression (transcript and ribosome footprints) of genes associated with the phosphate (PHO) regulon, in the tRNA thiolation mutant cells (uba4Δ and ncs2Δ), compared to WT cells, at the transcript and ribosome-footprint levels (log2 2-fold changes).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq and ribosome profiling showing ~20 PHO regulon genes strongly downregulated (p<10−7) in uba4Δ and ncs2Δ cells (Figure 4E, 4F).

claim: The downregulation of PHO-related genes in thiolation mutants is exceptionally significant compared to other genes across the genome.
source: A density plot with a statistical comparison between WT and tRNA thiolation mutants, for changes in transcript or ribosome footprints of all genes in the genome, or only the PHO regulon. Note: p<10−7 for all the comparison datasets.
evidence: Statistical analysis of RNA-seq and ribosome profiling data showing p<10−7 for PHO regulon changes compared to genome-wide changes (Figure 4F).

claim: Gcn4 translation is increased in tRNA thiolation mutant cells based on ribosome profiling data.
source: Gcn4 translation is increased in tRNA thiolation mutant cells. Ribosome occupancy for the GCN4 ORF and its four upstream ORFs (uORFs) (represented by grey boxes) present in the 5' UTR are shown.
evidence: Demonstrated by ribosome profiling data showing increased ribosome occupancy on the GCN4 ORF in thiolation mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).

claim: Gcn4 mRNA is unchanged in tRNA thiolation mutant cells.
source: Gcn4 mRNA is unchanged in tRNA thiolation mutant cells. mRNA reads for the GCN4 ORF and its four upstream ORFs (uORFs) (represented by grey boxes) present in the 5' UTR are shown.
evidence: Shown by RNA-seq data demonstrating similar mRNA read coverage for GCN4 in WT and thiolation mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).

claim: Pho12 and Pho84 proteins are decreased in tRNA thiolation mutants.
source: Pho12 and Pho84 proteins are decreased in tRNA thiolation mutants.
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis showing substantially reduced Pho12-FLAG and Pho84-FLAG protein levels in uba4Δ and ncs2Δ cells compared to WT (Figure 5B).

claim: Pho84 protein is decreased in tRNA thiolation mutants in both high and low Pi conditions.
source: Pho84 protein is decreased in tRNA thiolation mutants in both high and low Pi conditions.
evidence: Shown by Western blot analysis demonstrating reduced Pho84-FLAG levels in uba4Δ and ncs2Δ cells compared to WT in both high and low phosphate media (Figure 5C).

claim: Acid phosphatase activity is decreased in tRNA thiolation mutants.
source: Acid phosphatase activity is decreased in tRNA thiolation mutants.
evidence: Measured by colorimetric assay showing significantly reduced acid phosphatase activity in uba4Δ cells compared to WT in both high and low Pi conditions (Figure 5D).

claim: Trehalose amounts are increased upon phosphate starvation.
source: Trehalose amounts are increased upon phosphate starvation.
evidence: Measured by colorimetric assay showing significantly increased trehalose content in WT cells grown in no Pi media compared to high Pi media (Figure 6A).

claim: Gcn4 protein is increased upon phosphate starvation.
source: Gcn4 protein is increased upon phosphate starvation.
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis showing increased Gcn4-HA protein levels in WT cells grown in no Pi media compared to high Pi media (Figure 6B).

claim: GCN4 translation is Gcn2-dependent in phosphate-starved wild-type cells.
source: GCN4 translation is Gcn2-dependent in phosphate-starved wild-type cells.
evidence: Shown by luciferase assays demonstrating that gcn2Δ cells do not show increased Gcn4-luciferase activity upon phosphate starvation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claim: Cells lacking Uba4 and Gcn4 also show decreased acid phosphatase activity.
source: Cells lacking Uba4 and Gcn4 (uba4Δ gcn4Δ) also show decreased acid phosphatase activity.
evidence: Measured by colorimetric assay showing that uba4Δ gcn4Δ double mutant has significantly decreased acid phosphatase activity similar to uba4Δ alone (Figure 6C).

claim: Loss of Gcn4 alone has no effect on acid phosphatase activity.
source: Acid phosphatase activity was determined in WT, tRNA thiolation mutant (uba4Δ), gcn4Δ, uba4Δ gcn4Δ, pho4Δ and pho80Δ grown in high Pi media conditions supplemented with amino acids, by a colorimetric assay. Note that loss of Gcn4 alone has no effect on acid phosphatase activity.
evidence: Demonstrated by acid phosphatase assay showing similar activity in gcn4Δ and WT cells (Figure 6C).

claim: Intracellular Pi levels are maintained in tRNA thiolation mutant cells by Tps2 activity.
source: Intracellular Pi levels are maintained in tRNA thiolation mutant cells (uba4Δ) by Tps2 activity.
evidence: Demonstrated by colorimetric assay showing that uba4Δ tps2Δ double mutant has dramatically reduced intracellular Pi levels (~65%) compared to either single mutant (Figure 7B).

claim: There is a synthetic genetic interaction between TPS2 and tRNA thiolation genes at 37°C.
source: Synthetic genetic interaction between TPS2 and tRNA thiolation genes (UBA4 and NCS2) at 37° C.
evidence: Demonstrated by spotting assay showing strong synthetic growth defect in uba4Δ tps2Δ and ncs2Δ tps2Δ double mutants at 37°C (Figure 7C).

claim: There is a synthetic genetic interaction between PHO80 and tRNA thiolation genes.
source: Synthetic genetic interaction between PHO80 and tRNA thiolation genes (UBA4 and NCS2).
evidence: Shown by spotting assay demonstrating severe synthetic growth defect in pho80Δ uba4Δ and pho80Δ ncs2Δ double mutants (Figure 7D).

claim: The loss of tRNA thiolation results in hypersensitivity to oxidative agents and the TORC1 inhibitor rapamycin.
source: The loss of tRNA thiolation results in hypersensitivity to oxidative agents, and the TORC1 inhibitor rapamycin (Fichtner et al., 2003; Goehring et al., 2003a; Goehring et al., 2003b; Laxman and Tu, 2011; Scheidt et al., 2014), suggesting a role for thiolated tRNAs in maintaining metabolic homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Several studies have observed that a loss of tRNA thiolation alters amino acid homeostasis, and the amino-acid starvation regulator Gcn4 is induced.
source: More pertinently, several studies have observed that a loss of this modification alters amino acid homeostasis, and the amino-acid starvation regulator Gcn4 is induced (Laxman et al., 2013; Zinshteyn and Gilbert, 2013; Nedialkova and Leidel, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Thiolated tRNAs are required to maintain metabolic cycles in yeast.
source: Further, thiolated tRNAs are required to maintain metabolic cycles in yeast (Laxman et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The amounts of thiolated tRNAs reflect the intracellular availability of sulfur-containing amino acids and couple the sensing of amino acid sufficiency with growth.
source: Finally, the amounts of thiolated tRNAs reflect the intracellular availability of sulfur-containing amino acids (cysteine and methionine), and couple the sensing of amino acid sufficiency with growth (Laxman et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Nucleotide limitation can directly induce Gcn4.
source: Notably, early studies have shown that nucleotide limitation can itself directly induce Gcn4 (Rolfes and Hinnebusch, 1993), suggesting that the increased Gcn4 amounts could be due to this.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Increased mRNA levels of nucleotide biosynthetic genes in thiolation mutants may be due to feedback upregulation in response to reduced nucleotides.
source: Indeed, increased mRNA levels of nucleotide biosynthetic genes observed in thiolation mutants may be due to feedback upregulation in response to reduced nucleotides, which is also a well-established phenomenon (Davis and Ares, 2006; Kwapisz et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and inference from the observed data.

claim: Earlier studies have noted a strong correlation of phosphate starvation with decreased nucleotide synthesis and ATP availability.
source: Earlier studies have noted a strong correlation of phosphate starvation with decreased nucleotide synthesis, and ATP availability (Boer et al., 2010; Klosinska et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Reduced ATP synthesis is a hallmark of phosphate starvation.
source: Reduced ATP synthesis is a hallmark of phosphate starvation (Boer et al., 2010), along with increased trehalose synthesis (discussed in a subsequent paragraph).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Studies have observed that trehalose increases upon phosphate starvation.
source: Studies have observed that trehalose increases upon phosphate starvation (Lillie and Pringle, 1980; Klosinska et al., 2011), and TPS2 is upregulated (Ogawa et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In phosphate starvation conditions, central carbon metabolism is down, and phosphate limitation is a 'general starvation' cue.
source: In these conditions, central carbon metabolism is down, and phosphate limitation is a 'general starvation' cue (Brauer et al., 2008; Boer et al., 2010; Gurvich et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Trehalose synthesis determines flux through the pentose phosphate pathway and nitrogen metabolism in pathogenic fungi.
source: These data also explain earlier observations from pathogenic fungi, showing that that trehalose synthesis determines flux through the pentose phosphate pathway, and nitrogen metabolism (Wilson et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Phosphate starvation results in better cell survival in limited nutrient conditions and promotes efficient recovery when nutrients become available.
source: Additionally, phosphate starvation results in better cell survival in limited nutrient conditions, and also promotes efficient recovery when nutrients become available (Gurvich et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Trehalose accumulation and utilization are tightly coupled with exit from and re-entry into the cell division cycle.
source: Since trehalose accumulation and utilization are respectively tightly coupled with exit from and re-entry into the cell division cycle (Shi et al., 2010; Shi and Tu, 2013), we propose a dual role for trehalose synthesis during phosphate-limitation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Trehalose plays roles in cell survival during desiccation and freezing.
source: These include cell survival during desiccation and freezing (Calahan et al., 2011; Erkut et al., 2011; Erkut et al., 2016; Tapia and Koshland, 2014; Tapia et al., 2015), the ability to act as a protein chaperone (Tapia and Koshland, 2014), and as a membrane protectant (Abusharkh et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Trehalose can act as a protein chaperone.
source: These include cell survival during desiccation and freezing (Calahan et al., 2011; Erkut et al., 2011; Erkut et al., 2016; Tapia and Koshland, 2014; Tapia et al., 2015), the ability to act as a protein chaperone (Tapia and Koshland, 2014), and as a membrane protectant (Abusharkh et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Trehalose acts as a membrane protectant.
source: These include cell survival during desiccation and freezing (Calahan et al., 2011; Erkut et al., 2011; Erkut et al., 2016; Tapia and Koshland, 2014; Tapia et al., 2015), the ability to act as a protein chaperone (Tapia and Koshland, 2014), and as a membrane protectant (Abusharkh et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Previous studies have observed decreased phosphate-related transcripts in tRNA thiolation deficient cells.
source: While previous studies have observed decreased phosphate-related transcripts in tRNA thiolation deficient cells (Leidel et al., 2009; Nedialkova and Leidel, 2015; Chou et al., 2017), possible roles for phosphate in tRNA thiolation mediated function have been ignored.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mutants of all U34 tRNA modifications show similar metabolic phenotypes as the thiolation mutants.
source: Mutants of all these related U34 tRNA modifications show similar metabolic phenotypes as the thiolation mutants (Zinshteyn and Gilbert, 2013; Nedialkova and Leidel, 2015; Chou et al., 2017; Han et al., 2018), and have a down-regulated PHO response (Chou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mutants of U34 tRNA modifications have a down-regulated PHO response.
source: Mutants of all these related U34 tRNA modifications show similar metabolic phenotypes as the thiolation mutants (Zinshteyn and Gilbert, 2013; Nedialkova and Leidel, 2015; Chou et al., 2017; Han et al., 2018), and have a down-regulated PHO response (Chou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The correlation of tRNA thiolation with growth and rewired metabolism is emerging in cancer development.
source: Intriguingly, this correlation of tRNA thiolation with growth and rewired metabolism is emerging in cancer development (McMahon and Ruggero, 2018; Rapino et al., 2018), suggesting possibly conserved metabolic roles for these modified tRNAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: The prototrophic CEN.PK strain of Saccharomyces cerevisiae was used in all experiments.
source: The prototrophic CEN.PK strain of Saccharomyces cerevisiae was used in all the experiments (van Dijken JP et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the experimental system used.

claim: Cells lacking TPS2 cannot complete trehalose synthesis and cannot release phosphate.
source: We directly tested the hypothesis that trehalose synthesis is a direct way for cells to restore internal phosphate in tRNA thiolation mutants, by utilizing cells lacking TPS2. These cells cannot complete trehalose synthesis, and importantly cannot release phosphate (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is based on biochemical knowledge of the Tps2 enzyme function and the experimental design.

claim: In cells lacking TPS2, intracellular Pi levels are lower relative to WT cells.
source: We first observed that in cells lacking TPS2 (tps2Δ) intracellular Pi levels were lower (~75–80%) relative to WT cells (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Measured by colorimetric assay of intracellular Pi levels.

claim: Tps2-mediated Pi release by dephosphorylation of trehalose-6-P is important for maintaining internal phosphate levels.
source: This suggests that while other pathways (phosphate uptake, glycerol production and vacuolar phosphate export) remain relevant, Tps2p-mediated Pi release by dephosphorylation of trehalose-6-P is itself important for maintaining internal phosphate levels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed reduction in Pi levels in tps2Δ cells.

claim: uba4Δ cells have only slightly reduced intracellular Pi levels relative to WT cells.
source: Importantly, uba4Δ cells had only slightly reduced intracellular Pi levels (~90%) relative to WT cells (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Measured by colorimetric assay of intracellular Pi levels.

claim: Cells lacking both thiolation and Tps2 show a dramatic reduction in Pi levels compared to either single mutant.
source: Contrastingly, the cells lacking both thiolation and Tps2 (uba4Δ tps2Δ) showed a dramatic reduction in Pi levels (~65%), compared to either of their single mutants.
evidence: Measured by colorimetric assay showing synergistic reduction in Pi levels in the double mutant.

claim: During phosphate limitation, trehalose synthesis concurrently releases Pi which restores phosphate balance in the cell.
source: During phosphate limitation, trehalose synthesis concurrently releases inorganic phosphate, which restores phosphate balance in the cell and diverts flux away from nucleotide synthesis and growth.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion based on the biochemical function of Tps2 and the experimental data showing the role of trehalose synthesis in maintaining Pi levels.

claim: When phosphate is no longer limiting, cells can liquidate trehalose to re-enter the cell division cycle, enabling rapid recovery.
source: When phosphate is no longer limiting, cells can liquidate trehalose to re-enter the cell division cycle, enabling rapid recovery.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the known role of trehalose in cell cycle regulation and the findings of this study.
